questions.stem: At an anthropometric design check, a supervisor proposes: "Conclude the task is safe if no employee reports pain during one observation". The underlying case is: A task involves moderate force, high repetition, awkward wrist posture, and little recovery time. Each factor alone appears tolerable. What is the best assessment? Which alternative is the most defensible correction?
options: Average the four factors so high and low values cancel each other
Assess only force because repetition and posture cannot interact with it
Evaluate the combined exposure because interacting risk factors can materially increase musculoskeletal risk
Conclude the task is safe if no employee reports pain during one observation
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Ergonomic risk is often driven by combinations of force, repetition, posture, duration, vibration, and recovery rather than one isolated threshold.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The proposed response 'Average the four factors so high and low values cancel each other' remains incomplete or misapplies the controlling ergonomic risk-factor interaction principle.
The proposed response 'Assess only force because repetition and posture cannot interact with it' remains incomplete or misapplies the controlling ergonomic risk-factor interaction principle.
The proposed response 'Conclude the task is safe if no employee reports pain during one observation' remains incomplete or misapplies the controlling ergonomic risk-factor interaction principle.

questions.stem: At a shift-schedule redesign, a supervisor proposes: "Design all dimensions for the largest worker regardless of reach". The underlying case is: A fixed control panel is designed around the average worker and is unreachable for many shorter employees. What design principle should replace the average-user approach? Which alternative is the most defensible correction?
options: Design reach requirements for an appropriate smaller percentile and clearances for an appropriate larger percentile, with adjustability where feasible
Require shorter workers to use improvised platforms instead of changing the design
Design all dimensions for the largest worker regardless of reach
Use the 50th percentile for every dimension because it represents most people
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Designing only for the average excludes substantial portions of the population. Reach and clearance require different percentile strategies and often adjustability.

The proposed response 'Design all dimensions for the largest worker regardless of reach' remains incomplete or misapplies the controlling anthropometric design principle.
The proposed response 'Use the 50th percentile for every dimension because it represents most people' remains incomplete or misapplies the controlling anthropometric design principle.

Adjust the workstation so shoulders are relaxed, elbows supported near a comfortable angle, wrists are neutral, and input devices are within easy reach
Move the keyboard farther away to encourage arm exercise
Raise the monitor further and ask the employee to type faster

questions.stem: At a workstation assessment, a supervisor proposes: "Issue thicker gloves and make no change to tools or exposure time".
